name: Golden Gate Bridge
label: Golden Gate Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Battery Spencer' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Battery Spencer' (way/111530592): middle (128 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/451971: large area 'Golden Gate Bridge' (2955 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The city's most famous landmark, best seen from the Presidio or Battery Spencer.

text.description: The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge across the Golden Gate, the strait about a mile wide where San Francisco Bay meets the Pacific. It opened on 27 May 1937 and carries road traffic as well as people on foot and on bikes. Back then it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world. The main span is 1,280 m, and the total height is 227 m. A travel guide has called it the most photographed bridge in the world, and guides call the view from Battery Spencer, on the Marin Headlands side at the north end of the bridge, the classic postcard view. From up here you look at the bridge nearly side-on and from above, with the north tower close by and San Francisco and the bay behind it. That layering of tower, span, water and city is why the view works so well on a phone. It is free, and the views are wide and open. If you want a second angle, Golden Gate Overlook shows the bridge head-on between two cypress trees, and Baker Beach shows it from the ocean side. Fog can hide the bridge completely, so check conditions before you set off.
text.geographic_location: The bridge links San Francisco, at the northern tip of the San Francisco Peninsula, to Marin County across the Golden Gate strait. The viewpoint is on the Marin Headlands side, at the north end of the bridge, looking back towards the city.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops near this viewpoint. The viewpoint is reached from Conzelman Road on the Marin Headlands side, which leads to Battery Spencer. Parking is very limited and busy at weekends, so walk from the Battery Spencer car park rather than relying on the road turnouts. In summer, traffic may force a detour via McCullough Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower, the span and the city behind in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the north tower or to bring the city skyline closer to the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Battery Spencer (Marin Headlands side, on the north end of the bridge, reached from Conzelman Road). The bridge seen nearly side-on from above, with the north tower close and San Francisco and the bay behind it. Stay behind any barriers and keep clear of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical line so the bridge doesn't look tilted. Let the span run diagonally across the frame, with the city in the gap behind it. Keep a bit of the headland in a corner to give a sense of height. For a different angle, Golden Gate Overlook gives a head-on view between two cypress trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the paint keep their detail. If fog is rolling through, take a Live Photo and pick the best moment afterwards. Wipe the lens before you start, as sea air can leave it smeary.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or early morning, or sunset, when fog or soft light makes the bridge stand out.

text.access_note: Battery Spencer is a free, open viewpoint, but parking and road access can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Sea air can leave a smear on a phone lens, so wiping it before shooting helps.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep detail in a bright sky and the bridge paint.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit the tower, span and city into a single frame at this viewpoint.

name: Alcatraz Island
label: Alcatraz Island
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pier 39' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pier 39' (way/128240121): point nearest the subject (144 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20197830: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Alcatraz Island' (589 m across).
notes: Former prison island in the bay.

text.description: Alcatraz is a small, flat-topped rock about 1.25 miles offshore in San Francisco Bay, and it is one of the most recognisable shapes on the water. It began as a lighthouse site and a military fort, and from 1934 it was a federal prison. The prison closed on 21 March 1963. Today the island is run by the National Park Service and is a National Historic Landmark. It still has the oldest operating lighthouse on the West Coast, and nearly 1.4 million people visit each year. The island is only a little over 500 metres long, so from the mainland it reads as a compact shape sitting on open water. That makes it easy to frame cleanly, with the sky and bay around it. The best-placed view is from Pier 39. Walk out to the far, back side, past the sea lions, where the angle is most open and the island sits centred across the water. Zoom in rather than shooting wide, because the island looks tiny at normal zoom. Fog can hide it completely, so have a look at the bay before you walk all the way out. If you want a wider view that includes the Golden Gate Bridge, try Marina Green instead.
text.geographic_location: Alcatraz Island sits in San Francisco Bay, north of the city's waterfront and close to the Golden Gate strait.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Pier 39 on the waterfront. Once on the pier, walk to the far (back) side, past the sea lions. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens at 2x to 3x, whichever your phone offers. The default lens (1x) leaves the island small in a big empty frame, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) makes it smaller still.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pier 39 (far (back) side of the pier, past the sea lions). Alcatraz sits centered across open water, with the bay and sky spread behind it, shot best with a 2x to 3x phone zoom or a longer lens. Face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the island on the centre or lower-third line, with plenty of sky above. Keep the horizon level. Zoom in until the island fills a good part of the frame without the edges looking cramped. If you want a wider view, Marina Green shows the island with the Golden Gate Bridge and Angel Island in the same scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the island to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the island does not wash out. Hold the phone steady against a rail or your body at 2x to 3x to avoid blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour or early morning gives the warmest light. Midday in summer can look harsh. Fog can hide the island at any time, so be ready to try again.

text.access_note: Pier 39 is a public waterfront pier, but visiting Alcatraz itself needs a ferry and may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fisherman's Wharf
label: Fisherman's Wharf
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hyde Street Pier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hyde Street Pier' (way/25319880): point nearest the subject (214 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11283438662: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fisherman's Wharf'.
notes: Waterfront district with the famous sign and sea lions nearby.

text.description: Fisherman's Wharf is the busy stretch of San Francisco's northern waterfront. It began as a working fishing port, and in 1900 the state set this shoreline aside for commercial fishing boats. The fishing docks declined in the 1960s and 1970s as tourism took over, but a few old family-run seafood restaurants are still here. For a phone camera, the best frame is not one single landmark. It is the mix of historic ships, the bay and the waterfront buildings. From here you can look southwest towards Ghirardelli Square and the waterfront, with the old ships moored close by. Across the water you can also pick out the Golden Gate Bridge. The main tourist strip of the Wharf, along Jefferson Street, lies to the east. Pier 39, with its sea lion colony, is further along the same waterfront. The pier has been reported closed for renovation, so check its status before you go. If the entrance is closed, the lettered Fisherman's Wharf sign or Aquatic Park both make good alternatives. Aquatic Park has a sheltered cove, a curved pier and a Streamline Moderne bathhouse, with the bay beyond.
text.geographic_location: Fisherman's Wharf is on San Francisco's northern waterfront, north of Russian Hill, North Beach and Telegraph Hill.
text.directions_text: The Powell / Hyde cable car line ends at Aquatic Park, on the western side of the Wharf. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view towards Ghirardelli Square and the waterfront. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the ships' masts and rigging. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Golden Gate Bridge across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hyde Street Pier (pier entrance, looking southwest). Ghirardelli Square and the waterfront from the pier entrance, with the historic ships of the maritime park nearby. The main Wharf is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterfront along the top third of the frame. Keep a ship's hull or rigging in the foreground for depth. Turn to the water for a second shot of the Golden Gate Bridge. For a different view, Aquatic Park gives a calm cove with the curved pier and bathhouse in the foreground. The Fisherman's Wharf sign gives a street-level shot with the busy Wharf behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ships to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and water keep their colour. Wipe the lens first, as sea air can leave a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the waterfront. Early morning is typically quieter if you want the ships without people.

text.access_note: The Hyde Street Pier is part of a national park site and has been reported closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer on the waterfront.
Early morning is typically quieter than midday at the Wharf.
Sea air can leave a film on a phone lens.

name: Lombard Street
label: Lombard Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Leavenworth Street' (5 web pages); placed at crossing of Leavenworth Street and Lombard Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4972243722: the OpenStreetMap point 'Lombard Street'.
notes: The famously winding block on Russian Hill.

text.description:
Lombard Street is famous for one steep block on Russian Hill that zigzags down the slope in eight sharp hairpin bends. The bends were built in 1922 to soften a natural 27 percent grade that was too steep for most vehicles. The block is about 180 metres long, one-way downhill and paved with red bricks. Flower beds and houses sit between the curves, and that is what makes it so photogenic.

The view most people picture is from the bottom, looking uphill. From the foot of the block you can fit the whole stack of bends, the flowers and the houses into one frame. The street is busy with visitors, around two million a year as of 2015, so early morning gives you the best chance of a clear view. It is also a residential street, so keep to the sidewalk, stay out of the flower beds and don't block driveways.

If you want a different angle, the crest at Hyde Street has the top of the crooked block in the foreground, with Coit Tower and the bay beyond. A Powell-Hyde cable car sometimes passes there. For a quieter, more distant view, try the corner of Lombard Street and Grant Avenue, with North Beach rooftops and Coit Tower nearby.
text.geographic_location: Lombard Street's crooked block is on Russian Hill in San Francisco, between Hyde Street and Leavenworth Street. The Leavenworth end is the lower, eastern end.
text.directions_text: There is no station or stop at this spot, so walk to the corner of Lombard Street and Leavenworth Street, at the bottom of the crooked block. The Powell-Hyde cable car stops at the top of the block on Hyde Street, and from there you can walk downhill to the east on the sidewalk or the stairs. Allow extra time, as traffic around the street can be slow. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole run of bends. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the curves and flower beds. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can help if you want more of the houses and sky, but it makes the hill look smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Leavenworth Street and Lombard Street (bottom (east) end of the crooked block, on the sidewalk, looking uphill). The full stack of switchback curves, flower beds and houses rising up the hill in a single frame. Stay on the sidewalk, away from the road and crosswalk.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the street's upright centre line balanced, with the top bend near the upper third of the frame. Wait for a gap in the people and cars on the bends before you take the shot. For a different view, try the Hyde Street crest, where Coit Tower and the bay appear behind the top of the block.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the street to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky from washing out the red bricks and flowers. A Live Photo can catch a car coming down the bends.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: This is a public residential street with no entry ticket needed; stay on the sidewalks and stairs, and check local signs and the city's official site before you go, as drone use is restricted.
claims_not_in_sources: A telephoto lens (2x-5x) gives a tighter, more compressed view of the curves than the default lens.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes the hill look smaller in the frame.
Early morning is the best time to avoid people in the frame.
Traffic around the street can be slow, so allow extra time.

photo.artist: The original uploader was Y6y6y6 at English Wikipedia.

name: Ghirardelli Square
label: Ghirardelli Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aquatic Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Aquatic Park Historic District' (way/32839638): middle (535 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27104863: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ghirardelli Square' (174 m across).
notes: Former chocolate factory with its famous sign.

text.description: Ghirardelli Square is a cluster of old red-brick buildings at the foot of Russian Hill, beside the Aquatic Park Historic District and a short stroll from Fisherman's Wharf. Domenico Ghirardelli bought the whole city block in 1893 for his chocolate company. In 1964 it reopened as a restaurant and shopping complex, the first major re-use project of its kind in the United States. The big Ghirardelli sign was turned round to face the waterfront, so it greets you from the water side. That is why this view works so well: you get the sign and the brick buildings together in one frame. The best wide shot is from Aquatic Park, across the street on the waterfront side. Hyde Street Pier is a second option. It gives a sweeping view back across the water, with the historic ships in the foreground. Keep to the pier edge for that shot. Go around sunset if you can, when the bay turns gold and the sign comes on. The square is busy at most times, so wait a moment for gaps in the crowd before you take the picture.
text.geographic_location: Ghirardelli Square is on San Francisco's northern waterfront, at the foot of Russian Hill and next to the Aquatic Park Historic District. It is close to Fisherman's Wharf.
text.directions_text: From there the square is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot. Walk towards the sign and the brick buildings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sign and buildings together. If the square looks small and far away, try the telephoto lens (2x or more) to pick out the sign and brickwork. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and foreground, because the square will shrink in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Aquatic Park (across the street from the square, on the waterfront side). A wider view of the Ghirardelli sign and complex with the bay, sailboats and sometimes Alcatraz and the Golden Gate Bridge behind. Face south-west and you will see the Ghirardelli sign and the brick complex in front of you, with the bay behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the sign on one of the upper third lines, with the brick buildings below it. Keep the horizon level. For a different angle, Hyde Street Pier looks back across the water to the square with the historic ships in the foreground. Keep to the pier edge for that shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the evening sky keeps its colour and the sign does not burn out. After dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the bay turns gold and the sign comes on.

text.access_note: Aquatic Park and the square are public waterfront spaces. Hyde Street Pier is part of a national historic park. Boarding the historic ships there is ticketed, and you do not need to board them for the photo.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is busy at most times, so waiting for gaps in the crowd helps.
The ultra-wide lens makes distant subjects look smaller in the frame.
Night mode works best with the phone held steady against a railing or your body.
Looking south-west from Aquatic Park puts the square in front of you.

name: Pier 39
label: Pier 39
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'K-Dock' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'I Dock' (way/555946338): middle (4 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1856083: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pier known for its sea lions on the docks.

text.description: Pier 39 is a busy shopping and entertainment pier on San Francisco's waterfront, and for most visitors the star attraction is the California sea lions lazing on the floating docks beside it. That is what makes it photograph well: the animals pile up, doze, bark and shove each other, with the pier's sign and the bay behind them. The pier opened on 4 October 1978. The first sea lions hauled out on its docks in September 1989, and they have been drawing crowds ever since. Numbers change a great deal through the year. As many as 1,700 were reported in Thanksgiving week 2009, and in May 2024 the reported maximum was 1,100 to 1,200. In summer many head off to breed, so the docks can be much emptier. Look for the sea lions on the docks with the pier sign or the bay behind them. For a second picture, try the Musical Stairs, where the piano-key design is framed by the wooden pier and the people walking through it. On a clear day the wider views take in Alcatraz and the Golden Gate Bridge, though from the docks the bay and skyline are the more natural backdrop. Keep behind the barriers and let your phone's zoom do the work.
text.geographic_location: Pier 39 is on the edge of the Fisherman's Wharf district on San Francisco's northern waterfront. It is close to North Beach, Chinatown and the Embarcadero.
text.directions_text: Head for Fisherman's Wharf, at the edge of which Pier 39 sits. The historic F Market streetcars serve the area. The subject point is a very short walk to the north-east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the sea lions on the docks. Use the default lens (1x) for the sea lions with the pier sign and bay behind them. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the Musical Stairs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on K-Dock (west side of Pier 39, along the sea lion docks). The sea lions hauled out on the floating docks, with the pier's sign and the bay or skyline behind them. The pier itself is a short way to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the sea lions in the lower third, with the sign or skyline filling the upper part. Zoom in rather than leaning over the barriers. For a different shot, take the Musical Stairs with the ultra-wide, using the wooden pier and passing people as a frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the nearest sea lion to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the bright water or sky washes out the animals' fur. Try Live Photos to catch a bark or a shuffle, and hold the phone steady with both hands when you zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 10am, when the sea lions are most active and the pier is likely to be quieter. Numbers are highest from autumn through early spring.

text.access_note: The pier is a public waterfront attraction with shops and restaurants, but some attractions on it may be ticketed, and the sea lion viewing area may change, so check the official site before you go.

The pier is often quieter before about 10am.

name: Oracle Park
label: Oracle Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'China Basin Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'China Basin Park' (way/27656676): middle (280 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7325085: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oracle Park' (347 m across).
notes: Baseball stadium on the bay.

text.description: Oracle Park is the home of the San Francisco Giants baseball team, on the waterfront in the South Beach neighbourhood. It opened on 31 March 2000 and has had several names over the years, including Pacific Bell Park and AT&T Park, before Oracle bought the name in 2019. It photographs well because the ballpark sits right on the water. The stretch of bay beyond its right-field wall is unofficially called McCovey Cove, after the former Giants player Willie McCovey. From China Basin Park, directly across the cove, you can fit the stadium's right-field side, the water, the Bay Bridge and the downtown skyline into one frame. That is why it works so well on a phone: there is a foreground, a main subject and a backdrop. Take your time with the composition, as the water gives you a clean, uncluttered front edge. If you want a different angle, Lefty O'Doul Bridge gives a close view with the stadium beside it. Willie Mays Plaza has the statue in front of the main entrance, which makes a classic welcome-to-the-ballpark shot. The cove can look especially good in the evening, when the ballpark and bridge are lit. On match days the area is busy, so expect people walking through your frame. Lefty O'Doul Bridge is a drawbridge, so the view can be briefly interrupted when it opens.
text.geographic_location: Oracle Park is on the San Francisco Bay waterfront in the South Beach neighbourhood, beside McCovey Cove and the China Basin area.
text.directions_text: The Muni Metro 2nd and King Station is directly outside the ballpark, and the 4th and King Caltrain station is about a block and a half from it. A taxi to the ballpark area also works if you would rather not walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the cove, the ballpark and the bridge together. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the plaza is crowded and you want to keep the water in front. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the stadium and the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in China Basin Park (south shore of McCovey Cove, across the water from the ballpark). The stadium's right-field side with McCovey Cove in the foreground, and the Bay Bridge and downtown skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water along the bottom third of the picture. Place the stadium on one side and let the bridge and skyline fill the rest. Try to keep the horizon level. If you have time, also try Lefty O'Doul Bridge for a close shot with the stadium beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or rail so the lights come out sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening, when the light is softer and the ballpark and bridge are lit up. Match days are busy, so go earlier or on a non-match day if you want a clearer view.

text.access_note: China Basin Park is a public park, and the Bay Trail and waterfront areas are open to walkers. The area is busy on game days.

The area around the park and ballpark is busy on game days.

name: Palace of Fine Arts
label: Palace of Fine Arts
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palace of Fine Arts' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Palace of Fine Arts' (way/288371295): middle (94 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/288371295: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace of Fine Arts' (94 m across).
notes: Rotunda and lagoon in the Marina District.

text.description:
The Palace of Fine Arts is a domed rotunda with curved colonnades, standing beside a small lagoon in San Francisco's Marina District. Bernard Maybeck designed it for the 1915 Panama–Pacific International Exposition as a make-believe Roman ruin. It is the only structure from that fair still standing on its original site. The first version was built from wood and plaster, so it was completely rebuilt in concrete between 1964 and 1974. The open rotunda is about 49 metres (162 feet) high.

It photographs well because the lagoon was planned as a mirror, a stretch of still water that doubles the buildings. Water and trees frame the view, which is the classic wide shot of the palace. On a calm day the dome reflects clearly, and one guide says that is when the reflection works best.

Keep your phone low and level, and use the gridlines to keep the colonnade straight. For a different picture, stand close to the dome and tilt the phone up to catch its curved stone base. The Lyon Street Steps give a higher view down over the grounds and lagoon, but check the angle on site. Weddings and photo crews are often around the lagoon and colonnades, so be patient and wait for a gap.
text.geographic_location: In San Francisco's Marina District, around a small lagoon next to the large curved exhibition hall behind the rotunda.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Marina District and the Palace of Fine Arts lagoon. Once you reach the lagoon, walk round to the bank opposite the rotunda. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view of rotunda, colonnades and reflection. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if trees or the water's edge stop you stepping back, and keep the horizon level so the columns don't lean. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Palace of Fine Arts (opposite bank of the lagoon, facing the rotunda). The rotunda and colonnades mirrored in the lagoon, framed by the water and surrounding trees. Look west across the water, with the rotunda ahead of you and the colonnades curving to either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the rotunda just off-centre and let the water fill the lower third so the reflection is part of the picture. Let the trees frame the sides. If you want something different, go close to the dome and shoot upwards with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the dome and its curved stone base. The Lyon Street Steps are another option for a higher view over the lagoon.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines to line up the colonnade and horizon. Tap the rotunda to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Avoid Live Photos or motion modes if the wind is rippling the water, as the reflection will look broken.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday early mornings or late afternoons tend to be quieter, and a calm day gives the clearest reflection. Wind can spoil it.

text.access_note: The lagoon and its surroundings are used as a public park, but the exhibition hall behind is an events venue, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bay Bridge
label: Bay Bridge
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OSM N7216367686 (View on Golden Gate Bridge & Richardson Bay): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Double-deck bridge to Oakland, lit at night.

text.description: This spot is a viewpoint marked on the map, and the aim is a view of the scene ahead with the surroundings included, rather than a close-up. Views like this work best when the picture has a clear foreground, a middle layer and a distant layer. Something in the foreground, such as a railing, a wall or a patch of ground, gives the view a sense of scale. Keep the horizon level by switching on the gridlines. A distant subject can look small to the eye, so zoom in a little rather than leaving it as a thin line at the edge of a wide frame. Take a few shots with different amounts of sky, because the sky often decides whether the picture feels calm or busy. If people or vehicles are nearby, wait for a gap before you shoot, and keep clear of any road. Look at the screen before you shoot, since haze or reflections can flatten the view. Take one wide shot to show where you are, then a tighter one for the detail you like best.

name: Coit Tower
label: Coit Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lombard Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lombard Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28824850: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Coit Tower' (32 m across).
notes: Art Deco tower on Telegraph Hill with city views.

text.description:
Coit Tower is a slim Art Deco tower on top of Telegraph Hill, and it makes a good landmark for a phone photo because it stands out above the rooftops. It is 210 feet (64 m) tall and made of unpainted reinforced concrete, so it has a pale, simple look against the sky and the hillside. It stands in Pioneer Park and was built in 1932-33 with money left by Lillie Hitchcock Coit to beautify the city. Above the main entrance is a concrete relief of a phoenix, which is worth a close-up if you visit the tower itself.

From this distance the telephoto (2x-5x) is the lens to reach for.

Separately, guides suggest Lombard Street, on the crooked curves between Hyde Street and Leavenworth Street, well over a kilometre to the west of the tower. From there the tower rises above the flower-lined bends of the road, and guides list it as one of the more open, unobstructed angles on the tower. One guide notes that from this side you may need a clear day and a long lens, so on a phone, use the telephoto and wait for good visibility. Lombard Street is a busy public street, so keep to the pavement if you go.

For a different view, Pier 39 shows the tower on the hill behind the waterfront and the downtown skyline. The Filbert Street Steps frame it with terraced cottage gardens and trees, but they are a long, steep climb.
text.geographic_location: Coit Tower is on Telegraph Hill in San Francisco, in Pioneer Park, close to the North Beach area. Lombard Street (the crooked block between Hyde Street and Leavenworth Street) is a separate spot a good distance to the west.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport before you set out. From there the tower is 218 m to the south. Lombard Street, on the crooked block between Hyde Street and Leavenworth Street, is an optional separate viewpoint a good distance away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer, as you will be about 218 m away. The default lens (1x) shows more of your surroundings but makes the tower look small. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a wide scene with the tower small in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lombard Street (the crooked curves on the block between Hyde Street and Leavenworth Street). The tower rises above the crooked, flower-lined curves of the street, with the city and hillside around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, leaving the lower part of the picture for foreground. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. If you have time, Pier 39 gives a different view, with the tower on the hill behind the waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale concrete keeps its detail against the bright sky. Zoom in on the screen to check the tower is sharp before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a clear day. For the Lombard Street side, a guide notes you may need a clear day and a long lens. Check current conditions before you set out.

text.access_note: Lombard Street is an open public street, but the tower's observation deck and interior may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dragon Gate
label: Chinatown Dragon Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dragon Gate' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/65328703: the OpenStreetMap point 'Dragon Gate'.
notes: Entrance gate to Chinatown on Grant Avenue.

text.description:
The Dragon Gate marks the southern entrance to San Francisco's Chinatown, where Bush Street meets Grant Avenue. It was built in 1969 in the style of a traditional Chinese pailou, with three portals topped by green tiles, and was formally dedicated in October 1970. The tiles and the guardian lions were made and donated by Taiwan. It is described as the first permanent ceremonial gate in the United States, and it is one of the most photographed spots in Chinatown.

It works well on a phone because it gives you two different pictures. From across the junction you get the whole gate with Grant Avenue running away behind it. Close up, there is plenty of detail: the stone lions at the pedestrian portals, the roof tiles, and the dragons and fish along the top. The male lion, at the west portal, rests a paw on a pearl or stone. The female, at the east portal, has a paw on a young lion. Above the central portal are four Chinese characters, a motto attributed to Sun Yat-sen.

This stand-here point is right beside the lions, so use it for close-up shots and use the corner for the full gate. Keep to the pavement and crossings, as traffic runs along both streets.
text.geographic_location: The Dragon Gate stands at the junction of Bush Street and Grant Avenue, on the southern edge of Chinatown in San Francisco. It is the gateway you walk through to head north along Grant Avenue into the neighbourhood.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot. Start from Chinatown and head to the junction of Bush Street and Grant Avenue, where the gate spans Grant Avenue. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Chinatown gate at Grant and Bush. The phone icon on the map is at the foot of the gate, beside the stone lions. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the lions and the gate's base. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof tiles, dragons and inscriptions above you. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can squeeze in more of the gate if you step back, but it will stretch the edges, so keep the gate in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the gate is right in front of you. You can see the lions, roof tiles and inscriptions in close-up, which the wide view from the corner can't show. It is also a quieter spot than the crowded corner. For the full gate with all three portals, walk to the Grant Avenue and Bush Street corner and shoot up Grant Avenue into Chinatown.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and fill the frame with one lion, putting its face on a third line. Then tilt up and use telephoto to pick out the tiles and carved details. Take one wider shot from the corner, with the three portals centred and Grant Avenue leading away behind them. Look for people walking through the side portals, which shows the scale of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lion to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright sky is washing out the green tiles. Portrait mode can work on a lion for a softer background, but check the edges of the stonework. Take a few frames of each view, as passers-by often step into shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit at a less busy time if you want fewer people around the lions, and check the light when you arrive.

text.access_note: The gate stands over a public street and can be visited freely at any time, but keep to the pavement and crossings because of the traffic.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) tends to stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Transamerica Pyramid
label: Transamerica Pyramid
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Columbus Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Columbus Avenue and Kearny Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24222973: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Transamerica Pyramid' (88 m across).
notes: The pyramid-shaped skyscraper of the skyline.

text.description:
The Transamerica Pyramid is the slim, four-sided tower that gives San Francisco's skyline its sharpest point. It stands at 600 Montgomery Street in the Financial District. It has 48 storeys and reaches 853 feet (260 m). When it was finished in 1972 it was the tallest building in the city, and it kept that title until 2017. The pyramid shape was chosen to let more light reach the street below. It was not popular with everyone at first, but it is now treated as one of the city's symbols.

It photographs well because the building is so simple and so tall. The best view of it from this map comes from Columbus Avenue, where the street runs on a diagonal and leads your eye straight to the tower at the far end. Walking guides call this the best photo of the building. They also suggest waiting for fog to clear for a better shot.

Keep the street's edges and the spire both in the frame, and let the road lead into the picture. If you have time for a second view, Pier 7 shows the pyramid at the end of a row of old-style street lamps and railings, with the Bay Bridge behind you if you turn round. Columbus Avenue and Broadway gives a full view of the tower from further back, with the wide roadway keeping the frame clear. The tower's old observation deck is closed, so these street views are your best chance of a good photo.
text.geographic_location: The Transamerica Pyramid is in San Francisco's Financial District, at the northern edge of the area.
text.directions_text: No Underground stations or tram stops are close to this spot. It is a short walk from the Financial District, so head on foot for Columbus Avenue. Walk towards it down Columbus Avenue and the tower stays in view ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole street and the tower fit in the frame. Try 2x or 3x if your phone has a telephoto lens, to bring the spire closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the street, as it will make the tower look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Columbus Avenue and Kearny Street (Stand on the corner and face south down Columbus Avenue). The pyramid sits at the far end of Columbus Avenue, framed by the street's diagonal perspective.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with the centre of the street. Let the buildings on either side of the street act as the edges of the frame. Wait for a gap in the traffic and people if you can. As an alternative, Pier 7 gives a different view with the street lamps leading to the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white and the building keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, resting your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Wait for the fog to clear, as guides suggest, for a better shot. Visit in the morning or late afternoon, when the light on the tower changes.

text.access_note: Columbus Avenue is a public street, so you can take photos from there freely. The tower's observation deck is closed to the public.

name: Union Square
label: Union Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Union Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Union Square' (way/25278818): middle (157 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4609282251: the OpenStreetMap point 'Union Square'.
notes: Central plaza with the Dewey Monument and shopping.

text.description:
Union Square is a 2.6-acre public plaza in the middle of downtown San Francisco, ringed by department stores, hotels and shops. Its centrepiece is the Dewey Monument, a tall column topped by a statue of Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. The monument was dedicated in 1903 to Admiral George Dewey's victory at the Battle of Manila Bay. The square itself was set aside as a public space in 1850 and takes its name from the pro-Union rallies held here around the American Civil War. Underneath the lawns and the monument is an underground car park from around 1940, so you are standing on its roof.

It photographs well because the monument gives the wide, open plaza one clear focal point, with the busy facades around it as a backdrop. Street life adds interest, and in the festive season an ice rink and a large Christmas tree are set up, though these are seasonal, so check the square's calendar before you go. Stand north-west of the monument, look south-east across the plaza at the column and let the buildings frame it. Keep the phone level so the column stays upright, and wait for a gap in the crowd if you want a clean shot. If you want a quieter picture afterwards, Maiden Lane is a narrow pedestrian-only lane of boutiques and cafés with string lights overhead.
text.geographic_location: Union Square is in downtown San Francisco, in the central shopping, hotel and theatre district. The plaza is bordered by Geary, Powell, Post and Stockton Streets.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for downtown San Francisco and the shopping streets around Geary, Powell, Post and Stockton, or go by taxi and ask for Union Square. The plaza fills one city block, so it is easy to spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole plaza, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the monument. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the statue of Nike at the top of the column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Union Square (centre of the square, looking at the Dewey Monument). The Dewey Monument rising in the middle of the plaza, framed by the surrounding historic hotel and department-store facades and any seasonal decorations. From here the column rises ahead of you in the middle of the plaza, with the facades around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the monument on a centre or side line, with the facades filling the background. Keep the phone level so the column and buildings don't lean. For a different mood, Maiden Lane, a narrow pedestrian lane with string lights, makes a quieter second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky doesn't wash out. If people keep walking through, try a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour or sunset, when the light is warm on the monument and facades.

text.access_note: Union Square is an open public plaza, but events and seasonal attractions such as the ice rink may change what is open, so check the square's calendar before you go.

name: Japanese Tea Garden
label: Japanese Tea Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30900516: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Japanese Tea Garden' (209 m across).
notes: Garden with pagoda and arched drum bridge in Golden Gate Park.

text.description:
The Japanese Tea Garden is a small, calm corner of Golden Gate Park, with winding paths, ponds, stone lanterns, carefully pruned trees and a tea house. It began as a Japanese village built for the 1894 World's Fair and is now described as the oldest public Japanese garden in the United States. It covers about 3 acres, so you can see a lot in a short walk. The five-tiered pagoda was brought over from the 1915 Panama–Pacific Exposition. Makoto Hagiwara, who looked after the garden for most of the years between 1895 and 1925, is remembered in the name of the road beside it, Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive.

It photographs well because so much is packed into one frame: red pagodas, water, rocks and soft green foliage. The best-known view inside is the steep Drum Bridge (Taiko Bashi), whose reflection in the koi pond makes a full circle. It can be busy for long stretches, so expect people in your shots. From here you can frame the garden against its greenery without the crowds on the paths. Try a wide shot first, then a closer one picking out a single roof or tree. Parts of the garden have sometimes been closed or under restoration, so the view may differ from older photos.
text.geographic_location: In Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, beside the road named Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive. It is one of the three Gardens of Golden Gate Park, along with the San Francisco Botanical Garden and the Conservatory of Flowers.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for Golden Gate Park and the Japanese Tea Garden. Walk to Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, which runs along the garden's edge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the garden and its greenery together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single pagoda roof or lantern. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can stand back, as it can make the garden look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive. The garden as seen from the public road beside it, framed against its greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the tree line or rooftops along the upper third, with the road or path as a leading line in the foreground. Keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a second angle, the Drum Bridge and its circular reflection in the koi pond, or the grouped red pagodas above the pond, are worth a look from inside the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the foliage and red paintwork stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Turn on Live Photos if you want a few spare frames when people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, and soft morning light suits the greenery. Check the garden's hours first, as some views are inside and the opening times vary.

text.access_note: The view from Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive is from a public road, but the main views are inside the garden, which charges admission except during free early-morning hours on some days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fort Point
label: Fort Point
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Torpedo Wharf' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Torpedo Wharf' (relation/8346136): middle (154 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21597568: large area 'Fort Point National Historic Site' (879 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Brick fort directly under the Golden Gate Bridge.

text.description:
Fort Point is a brick fort tucked right under the southern end of the Golden Gate Bridge, so the steel arch seems to sit on top of it. The Spanish first fortified this headland in 1794. The fort you see today was built by the US Army just before the Civil War, with walls seven feet thick. To keep its guns close to the water, workers cut the 90-foot cliff down to 15 feet above sea level. It was the only fort of its kind on the West Coast. When the bridge was planned in the 1930s, the engineer Joseph Strauss changed his design so the fort could stay. It became a National Historic Site in 1970.

From here you see the whole bridge in one frame from near water level, with the pier rail and the bay in front. The fort lies a short walk to the west. If you want the dramatic look-up shot of the arch, go to the fort itself and shoot up past its brick walls. The Battery East Trail above the site is another option, with a view down onto the fort and across to the bridge. It is often very windy here, so hold your phone with both hands and keep a firm grip.
text.geographic_location: Fort Point sits on the southern side of the Golden Gate, at the entrance to San Francisco Bay. It lies directly below the southern end of the Golden Gate Bridge, next to Crissy Field.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach the Presidio area at the foot of the Golden Gate Bridge. Follow the shoreline towards the bridge and you will see the fort beneath its southern end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the pier to fit the whole bridge, the rail and the water into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arch and the fort's brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Torpedo Wharf (out onto the pier, between Fort Point and Crissy Field). A wider view of the whole bridge from near water level, with the pier's rail and the bay in the foreground. The fort lies to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge deck up with a horizontal line. Use the pier rail as a leading line towards the bridge. For a different view, go up to the fort's roof (if open) and shoot upwards at the underside of the steel arch with brick walls in the foreground, or try the Battery East Trail for a view down onto the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone in both hands, because wind makes it shake. Take a few shots of each frame so at least one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear spell when the bridge is not hidden by fog or low cloud. Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters the steel.

text.access_note: The fort's exterior and Torpedo Wharf are open-air public places, but the fort's interior and roof are open only on certain days, so check the official National Park Service site before you go.

name: Twin Peaks
label: Twin Peaks
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corona Heights Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Corona Heights Park' (way/225182880): middle (492 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17413960: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Twin Peaks' (194 m across).
notes: Hilltop viewpoint over the whole city.

text.description: Twin Peaks are two neighbouring hills near the geographic centre of San Francisco. At about 925 feet (282 m), they are the second and third highest natural points in the city. Only Mount Davidson is higher, by a few feet. The two summits, North and South, are roughly 200 m apart. This photo is of the peaks themselves, taken from the rocky summit of Corona Heights Park. From there you look south-west, and the peaks rise on the skyline with the city spread out below. It is a quieter place to stand than the top of Twin Peaks, and it lets you see the hills as a whole instead of looking out from them. The west-facing slopes of the peaks often catch fog and strong wind, so the view can change quickly. On a clear day the outline of the hills stands out well against the sky. Use the city below as foreground to give the picture some depth. The peaks are some way off, so a zoom lens will bring them closer. If you want a different angle, try the street-level view at 22nd Street and Collingswood Street, or the wide panoramas from Christmas Tree Point on the hill itself. Keep valuables out of sight if you leave a car anywhere near the hills, and check the weather before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Twin Peaks sits near the centre of San Francisco, and the neighbourhood around it shares the name.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options to Corona Heights Park, then walk up to the rocky summit. If you want to visit the peaks themselves, there is no public transport all the way to the top, but the 37 Corbett Muni line stops on Crestline Drive near a path up the hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the peaks closer and make them fill more of the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider shot with the city below. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the peaks look small and distant, so save it for a shot of the whole summit.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Corona Heights Park (summit, looking west toward the peaks). Twin Peaks rising on the skyline from the rocky summit of Corona Heights, with the city spread below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the peaks on the upper line, with the rooftops and streets filling the lower part of the frame. Include a little of the rocky summit in the foreground for depth. If you want another angle, the street-level view at 22nd Street and Collingswood Street, or the panoramas from Christmas Tree Point, are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the peaks to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its detail. If fog is rolling in, take a Live Photo as well, because moving cloud can make a good short clip. Hold the phone firmly in the wind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, as fog often hides the view, especially in the morning. Because you look south-west, the sun is behind you earlier in the day and in front of you in the evening, so the peaks will look flatter against the glare late on.

text.access_note: Corona Heights Park is a public park with no charge listed, but confirm access and conditions before you go.

name: Grace Cathedral
label: Grace Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Huntington Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Huntington Park' (way/32946958): middle (110 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W32946942 (Grace Cathedral): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Gothic Revival cathedral on Nob Hill.

text.description:
Grace Cathedral is a Gothic-style church whose front, with its tall spire, makes an easy and rewarding photo from the street. The classic angle is from Huntington Park, on the other side of Taylor Street. From there the whole facade sits in your frame, with the park's trees around the edges. That gives you a natural border and a feeling of depth that you don't get when you stand right at the door.

The cathedral also has a rose window above the front door. It is worth a second shot, either zoomed in from the park or from a different street. If you walk to Taylor Street, the window can look striking at dusk when it is lit against the darker facade, if the rose-window lighting is still switched on; check before planning a night shot. California Street gives a different view: the front and the rose window at an angle, with the cable car line and the street in the foreground. That adds a bit of San Francisco character to the picture.

The park is public, so you can take your time and try a few versions. Take one wide shot with the trees, one tighter shot of the spire and one of the rose window. Keep your phone upright for the full height of the spire, then turn it sideways for the wider scene. If the sky is bright, tap on the stonework rather than the sky so the facade doesn't turn dark.
text.geographic_location: Grace Cathedral is in San Francisco. Huntington Park, the best place for the photo, is a public park just across Taylor Street from the cathedral's front.
text.directions_text: Navigate to Huntington Park in San Francisco. Walk to the edge of the park facing the cathedral across Taylor Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the park to fit the facade and spire in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if trees or fences force you to stand close, and keep the building upright to avoid leaning edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and the top of the spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Huntington Park (east side of the park, facing west across Taylor Street). The front of the cathedral with its Gothic facade and spire, framed by the park's trees and seen from across the street. For a different view, try Taylor Street at dusk for the rose window if its lighting is still on, or California Street for an angled shot with the cable car line in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the spire with a vertical line so the building stands straight. Let a few tree branches frame the top or sides without covering the spire. An alternative is to cross to California Street and include the cable car line and the street in the foreground for an angled view of the front and rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone of the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the details of the stonework stay clear. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a tree, post or wall for the rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight suits the full view from the park, when the facade is clearly lit. Dusk is the time to try the lit rose window from Taylor Street, but the lighting may not be switched on, so be ready to enjoy the daylight shot instead.

text.access_note: Huntington Park is a public park with no fee for the view; for entering the cathedral itself, check the official site before you go.

name: Painted Ladies
label: Painted Ladies
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alamo Square Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Alamo Square' (way/745183964): middle (375 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/822484002: the OpenStreetMap point 'Painted Ladies'.
notes: Row of Victorian houses facing Alamo Square park.

text.description:
These are the Painted Ladies, a row of Victorian houses at 710-720 Steiner Street, facing Alamo Square Park. They are also called Postcard Row or the Seven Sisters. The developer Matthew Kavanaugh built them between 1892 and 1896. The bright multi-colour paint is much newer: San Francisco's colourful repaint movement began in the 1960s, and the 'painted ladies' name for these houses took off after a 1978 book. The row has appeared in an estimated 70 films, TV programmes and adverts, including the opening credits of Full House. That is why it feels so familiar.

It photographs well because the park slope lifts you high enough to line the pastel gables up against the downtown towers behind them. The classic frame is from the upper grassy slope on the west side of Steiner Street. Climb partway up and shift a few steps left or right until the towers clear the rooflines. Trees in front of the houses have grown and can hide some of the colours from lower down, so height helps. The skyline is often lost in fog, especially in summer, so keep a plain-houses version in mind as a backup. The houses are private homes, so photograph them only from the street and the park, and keep clear of the doorways.
text.geographic_location: The Painted Ladies stand on Steiner Street, on the east side of Alamo Square Park, in central San Francisco. The park's grassy slope faces them across the street.
text.directions_text: No nearby stations or stops are listed for this spot, so head to Alamo Square Park by whatever local route you prefer. The houses lie to the east, about 3 minutes on foot from there if you want to cross over for close-ups. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full row with the skyline behind. If the towers look small, try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring them closer to the roofs. Save the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you are close to the houses, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Alamo Square Park (upper grassy slope on the west side of Steiner Street, climbing toward the crest). The seven pastel Victorian houses in the foreground with the downtown towers rising above their rooftops. Move a few steps until the towers clear the roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the row across the lower third of the frame and let the towers fill the space above. Turn on the gridlines to keep the rooflines straight. For a different shot, walk down to Steiner Street. There you can get a diagonal view of the whole row with the park's greenery and part of the skyline. You can also take close-ups of the gables, trim, bay windows and paint colours.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail and the colours stay rich. Take a few frames as people walk through, and check which ones have a clear view of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when guides mention warm light on the facades. Early morning can be quieter. Fog often hides the skyline, especially in summer.

text.access_note: The park slope and the pavement are public places to view from, but the houses are private homes, so photograph them only from the street and the park.

name: Conservatory of Flowers
label: Conservatory of Flower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Conservatory Valley' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Conservatory Valley' (way/120480366): middle (127 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30675038: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Conservatory of Flowers' (85 m across).
notes: Victorian greenhouse in Golden Gate Park.

text.description:
The Conservatory of Flowers is a white Victorian greenhouse in Golden Gate Park, and it looks like a stage set for a postcard. A central dome rises nearly 60 feet (18 m), with curved glass wings spreading out on either side to an overall length of about 240 feet (73 m). Building work finished in 1879, which makes it the oldest building in the park. The wooden frame and glass are very pale, so they stand out well against the green lawn and trees.

The best-known view is from the lawn and formal flower beds in front, in Conservatory Valley. From here the whole symmetrical facade fits in one frame, and the flower beds and fountain in front add depth. The building sits on a gentle rise, so you look slightly up at it. This view also works when the building is closed. For a second angle, try John F Kennedy Drive for a wider, street-level view with the park's trees around the building. In season, Dahlia Dell gives you dahlia blooms in the foreground with the white building behind. Dahlia displays are seasonal, so what you see will vary.

Keep your phone level, use the gridlines to line up the centre of the dome, and take a few steps to either side to change how the flowers sit in front.
text.geographic_location: The Conservatory of Flowers is in Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, on a gentle rise overlooking Conservatory Valley.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head for Golden Gate Park and make your way to the Conservatory of Flowers. Face north and the conservatory is straight ahead. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full-building postcard shot. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the flower beds and fountain matter as much as the building, or use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the dome and cupolas.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Conservatory Valley (the lawn and formal garden beds directly in front of the building, facing the facade). The symmetrical white facade with its central dome and curved wings, framed by formal flower beds and a fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the dome on the centre line so both wings balance. Keep the phone level so the wings don't lean. Use the flower beds along the bottom of the frame to give depth. For something different, try the wider street-level view from John F Kennedy Drive, or Dahlia Dell for close-up blooms with the building behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the glass and paintwork don't wash out. Try panorama only if you can't fit both wings in at 0.5x, and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Right before sunset is the recommended time for outdoor photos here.

text.access_note: The lawn and flower beds in front are open park space, but entry to the building itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The main entrance and facade face south, so a viewer standing in front, looking north, will usually have the sun behind or beside them in the middle of the day.
The pale building may look overexposed on a phone in bright sun, so lowering the exposure slightly can help.

name: Ferry Building
label: Ferry Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Market Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Market Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/558731934: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'San Francisco Ferry Building' (247 m across).
notes: Historic terminal with clock tower on the Embarcadero.

text.description:
The Ferry Building is the long, arched waterfront building that closes off the end of Market Street, topped by a slim clock tower. The tower is 245 feet (75 m) tall and has four clock dials, each 22 feet (6.7 m) across. The architect A. Page Brown designed it in the Beaux-Arts style, and it opened in 1898. It has working ferry terminals, a food hall and offices, and it came through both the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes with little damage. For decades a freeway hid it from Market Street. Once the freeway came down, the view along the street was open again, and that view is the classic photo.

From here you get a close view of the tower and the end of Market Street, rather than the classic compressed shot. That classic view is taken from much further west up Market Street with a long lens, where the street's buildings frame the shot on both sides and the tower sits at the far end. The long arcade of arches along the front gives you a second, quieter photo if you step closer and go wide.

Saturday mornings bring a busy farmers market in front of the building. Crowds also gather before and after Giants games at nearby Oracle Park. Early morning or a weekday is easier. If you have time, Harry Bridges Plaza gives the front of the building with the Bay Bridge behind it.
text.geographic_location: On The Embarcadero, San Francisco's eastern waterfront, at the foot of Market Street and facing San Francisco Bay. It sits beside Embarcadero Plaza and Harry Bridges Plaza.
text.directions_text: Check local transport options for getting to the foot of Market Street on The Embarcadero. Golden Gate Ferry and San Francisco Bay Ferry routes also serve the building, if you are arriving by water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter crop of the tower. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you want more of the building and the end of the street in the frame. The compressed look of the street and tower together needs a spot much further up Market Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Market Street (a long way west up Market, facing the clock tower at the foot of the street). The clock tower closing off the end of Market Street, shot with a long lens so the street and tower look compressed together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the tower in the frame and turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Keep the foreground in the lower part of the frame so the tower sits above it. For a different view, try Harry Bridges Plaza for the front of the building with the Bay Bridge behind it. Pier 14 shows the tower from the bay side, but check its angle on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and clock faces keep their detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or a weekday is easiest, with fewer people in the way. Avoid Saturday mornings, when the farmers market is on, and the hours around Giants games.

text.access_note: The street view is from an open public street, but the ferry terminals, food hall and offices inside the building may have their own hours and rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Market Street is a busy street with traffic, so stand on the pavement while framing the shot.
